title: CBSE Class 1 Maths Pattern Worksheets: How to Teach Patterns (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: CBSE Class 1 Maths Pattern Worksheets + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach CBSE Class 1 Maths patterns the easy way: colour, shape and size patterns, what comes next, growing patterns and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Before a six-year-old adds or subtracts, they need to spot what repeats. Here is how I teach Class 1 patterns, from bangle colours to rangoli, with a quick quiz to check your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Watch a five-year-old thread beads — red, blue, red, blue — and you are watching the beginning of algebra. That sounds dramatic, but it is true. Long before a child can add 3 and 4, they can tell you that a red bead comes next. Patterns are the quiet first chapter of maths, and CBSE Class 1 Maths pattern worksheets exist to turn that instinct into a skill a child can name, extend and eventually invent.

In my experience teaching six-year-olds, patterns are the topic parents most often skip because they look like ‘just colouring’. They are not. A child who reads patterns confidently finds skip-counting, the multiplication tables and even odd-and-even numbers years later far easier. So it is worth slowing down here.

What a pattern actually is

A pattern is anything that repeats in a rule you can predict. The part that repeats is called the core (or unit). In red-blue-red-blue, the core is ‘red-blue’. Teach that one word early — once a child can point to the core, everything else follows, because ‘what comes next’ is simply the core starting again.

Class 1 patterns come in a few flavours. Do not rush through all of them in a week; let each one settle.

Colour patterns

The friendliest place to start. Bangles, beads, crayons, kolam dots — anything with two or three colours. Say the pattern out loud together: ‘green, yellow, green, yellow… so what is next?’ Reading a pattern aloud is half the learning.

Shape patterns

Circle, square, circle, square. Or triangle, triangle, circle — triangle, triangle, circle. Shape patterns push a child to look at form rather than colour, which is a genuine step up because colour is easier for young eyes to track.

Size patterns

Big, small, big, small. Or short-tall-short-tall using pencils. Size patterns feel obvious to adults but they teach comparison words — bigger, smaller, taller — that Class 1 needs anyway.

Reading the code: AB, ABB, ABC

You do not have to teach the labels, but they help you plan. An AB pattern (red-blue) is the simplest. An ABB pattern (red-blue-blue) is trickier because the core has three beads. An ABC pattern uses three different items. Move up only when the AB pattern is boringly easy.

What comes next — the heart of the worksheet

Most CBSE Class 1 Maths pattern worksheets are built around one question: what comes next? The skill is not guessing — it is finding the core, then continuing it. Teach your child to touch each item and whisper the pattern before answering. That touch-and-say habit stops the careless mistakes that come from eyeballing.

A small honest caveat: some worksheet patterns are ambiguous. ‘2, 4, 6, __’ could be a growing-by-two pattern (8) but a child might also see a repeat. If your child gives a sensible reason for a different answer, praise the reasoning — the thinking matters more than the boxed answer at this age.

Making their own patterns

Copying a pattern is Level 1. Extending it is Level 2. Creating one is Level 3, and it is where real understanding shows. Hand your child a bowl of buttons and ask them to make a pattern and tell you the rule. If they can say ‘two red, one white, two red, one white’, they truly get it. This step is often left out of worksheets, so add it yourself with objects from around the house.

Growing patterns — a gentle first taste

Repeating patterns stay the same size. Growing patterns get bigger by a rule: 1 step, 2 steps, 3 steps; or one dot, two dots, three dots. These are the seed of counting sequences and later of the times tables. Keep them simple in Class 1 — add one each time is plenty. You are planting a seed, not teaching arithmetic yet.

Everyday patterns to spot together

The best practice happens away from paper. Point patterns out in daily Indian life — children remember what they discover themselves.

  • Rangoli and kolam — almost every design repeats a motif; trace it with a finger.
  • Bangles and beads — colour patterns on a wrist or a mala.
  • Floor and wall tiles — ask which shape repeats.
  • Days of the week — the ultimate repeating pattern, seven long.
  • A saree or dupatta border — borders are patterns by design.

A simple weekly routine

Ten minutes beats an hour. Two days on colour patterns, two on shape and size, one on ‘make your own’, and the weekend for a mixed worksheet where the child has to decide the pattern type first. That deciding step — not being told which kind it is — is where fluency shows up. Do not chase speed; a child who can explain the core is in far better shape than one who fills boxes fast without knowing why.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly these ideas — colour, shape and size patterns, what comes next, and simple growing patterns. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable Class 1 workbook at the end has graded pattern pages with answer keys you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: CBSE Class 1 Patterns Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on colour, shape and size patterns, what comes next, and simple growing patterns. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: In the pattern red, blue, red, blue, red, __ , what comes next?
questions.explanation: The core is red-blue. After red, the core starts again with blue.

questions.q: What is the core (the repeating part) in circle, square, circle, square?
questions.explanation: The smallest part that repeats is circle-square.

questions.q: Big, small, big, small, big, __ . What comes next?
questions.explanation: The pattern alternates big and small, so after big comes small.

questions.q: Which of these is a growing pattern?
questions.explanation: 1, 2, 3, 4 gets bigger by one each time, so it is a growing pattern. The others repeat or stay the same.

questions.q: Triangle, triangle, circle, triangle, triangle, circle. What comes next?
questions.explanation: The core is triangle-triangle-circle. After a full core, it starts again with triangle.

questions.q: Clap, stamp, stamp, clap, stamp, stamp. What kind of core is this?
questions.explanation: One clap then two stamps is an ABB core — three parts with the second one repeated.

questions.q: Which set does NOT make a repeating pattern?
questions.explanation: 2, 5, 1, 8 has no repeating core, so it is not a pattern. The others all repeat.

questions.q: A child makes: one dot, two dots, three dots, __ dots. How many next?
questions.explanation: This growing pattern adds one dot each time, so after three comes four.

faq.q: Why do CBSE Class 1 Maths worksheets start with patterns?
faq.a: Patterns build the thinking that counting, skip-counting and later the multiplication tables depend on. Spotting what repeats teaches a child to predict using a rule — the same habit maths needs everywhere. It is also concrete and playful, so six-year-olds succeed early and stay confident.

faq.q: What types of patterns should a Class 1 child know?
faq.a: Repeating patterns by colour, shape and size (AB, ABB and ABC cores), being able to say what comes next, copying and creating their own pattern, and a first gentle taste of growing patterns like 1, 2, 3, 4. Mastery of the repeating kind matters most in Class 1.

faq.q: My child copies patterns but cannot make their own. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Not at all — copying comes first, then extending, then creating. Give them buttons or beads and ask them to build a pattern and say its rule out loud. Creating is the last step and often takes a few weeks of play to click.

faq.q: How can we practise patterns without worksheets?
faq.a: Spot them in daily life: rangoli and kolam designs, bangle colours, floor tiles, saree borders and the days of the week. Ask your child to trace the repeat with a finger and say it aloud. This everyday noticing sticks far better than paper alone.
